## Breaking changes

Every change listed here declares itself breaking — at `0.x` a breaking change takes the **MINOR**, so these are the only version steps that can break you. Rendered from the same flag the release advisor reads, so a declared break cannot be missing from it.

| version | change |
|---|---|
| [Unreleased](#unreleased) | the Node package requires Node >= 22. |
| [Unreleased](#unreleased) | `@laterite/ags4-wasm` is the slim engine — 757 KiB gzipped instead of 1.8 MB. |
| [0.10.0](#0100--2026-08-02) | `diff` and `censor` take an options object too. |
| [0.9.0](#090--2026-07-30) | every `@laterite/ags4-wasm` export takes an options object. |
| [0.9.0](#090--2026-07-30) | a synthesised `TRAN` is stamped by the caller, never invented. |
| [0.8.0](#080--2026-07-28) | Metadata synthesis is now opt-in. |
| [0.7.0](#070--2026-07-08) | The CLI binary and Python console-script are renamed `lat-check` → `lat`. |
| [0.6.0](#060--2026-07-04) | The 174 typed-graph classes moved to the `laterite.groups` submodule. |

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **`laterite` takes and returns AGS4 as text — `ags4::read_str`, `ags4::validate_str`, `Written::text`.** The facade could only be handed bytes, so a caller holding a `String` — a template, a database column, a literal — had to write `read_bytes(s.as_bytes())`. That worked, which is why it lasted: it is the workaround, not the door, and Python and Node both offer the door. The modality register (added in #241) is what made the absence legible rather than merely true. Text is a distinct source internally, not bytes wearing a hat, so `encoding` cannot reach it: applying a codepage to already-decoded text re-reads UTF-8 as cp1252 and turns `°` into `Â°`, corrupting exactly the cells the option exists to rescue. That is enforced structurally and asserted both ways — the text form is exempt, the bytes form still transcodes. `Written` now holds a `String` with bytes derived, the same way round as Python's `Ags4File`, so `text()` costs nothing; `bytes()` and `into_bytes()` are unchanged. Every case is asserted as EQUAL to the bytes path rather than merely working, because a convenience form that is a second implementation is a second set of bugs.
- **`laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` publish to crates.io at 0.9.0.** Both were prepared in full for the first publish and then held back by a single flag, so day one's frozen surface stayed as small as possible. That deferral is spent. They are new crates at the engine's existing number, so nothing moves to admit them: diff lands in publish wave 3, merge in wave 5, and the nine crates already on the registry are skipped rather than republished. What changes is not that the API is frozen — crates.io makes a *version* immutable, not a surface — but that `cargo semver-checks` and the public-API snapshot now police edits to these two. For merge that is the point worth stating: what publishes is `merge_parsed`, whose `&[ParsedFile]` shape is the one laterite#162 endorses, while the typed merge surface #162 warns about is not published and stays free to design. Both crates gained a README, because a published crate without one has a bare crates.io page and that is not recoverable for anyone who already looked.
- **`laterite::transport` — the Rust crate can compress and encrypt files.** `pack`/`unpack` (zstd) and `lock`/`unlock` (zstd + an age passphrase), each in a path form and a `_bytes` form that never touches a disk. The odd part is that this was already *linked*: the facade enables `laterite-ags4-core`'s default-on `transport` feature, so every Rust consumer has been carrying age and zstd in their dependency tree while being unable to call a single function through them. It sits at the crate ROOT rather than under `ags4`, because the envelope understands no format — it will compress a JPEG — and the root's rule is that it stays format-neutral. Same shared envelope as every other surface, so a Rust-sealed file opens with `lat unlock`, Python, Node, the browser, and stock `age` given the passphrase. The two password-carrying builders redact in `Debug`: a derived one would put the passphrase into any log line that rendered the builder, which no round-trip test would ever have noticed.
- **The Rust crate mints and consumes `.ags.idx` certificates.** `doc.certify().to_path(…)` / `.to_bytes()` mint one over a file that validates clean, and `ags4::validate(…).index(cert)` offers it back so the rule engine does not run. Spelled on **validate** rather than on read, because this crate's validate is a free function with no `Document::validate()` for a read-time cert to reach. A certificate is never auto-discovered — one sitting beside a file is not consent to trust it — and a stale one cannot produce a wrong verdict, only a slower one: the engine reruns and `Report::revalidate_reason()` says why. Minting is over the ORIGINAL source bytes, before any transcode, which is why `Document` now retains them; certifying the decoded form would mint a certificate that never matches its own file, and every ASCII test would still have passed.
- **A certificate can also make a Rust read skip the file.** `read(f).index(cert)).only(["LOCA"])` parses that group straight out of the byte range the certificate records and never looks at the rest of the delivery; `Document::sliced()` reports whether it did. This is deliberately NOT what `read(index=)` means on Python and Node — there a certificate parked on the handle lets a later `.validate()` skip the rule engine, which this facade has no `Document::validate()` to do. It declines rather than risks: a stale certificate, a group the index places in two sections (slicing the first would return a strict subset of its rows, silently), or a transcode that moved the offsets all fall back to the whole-file parse, which is always correct. `only()` on its own is still a plain filter.
- **The Rust crate repairs and builds — `ags4::fix` and `ags4::build`.** `fix` is the mechanical repair the browser fix UI runs, headless: from a path, bytes or text, applying the safe set (CRLF, BOM, embedded CR, short-row padding, numeric formatting, the `TRAN` delimiter rows) and re-validating its own output, so `Fixed::findings` is what could *not* be put right rather than what was wrong to begin with. It is non-destructive until you name a destination — in place is the source path passed to `to_path`, not a separate flag, because there is nothing a flag would express that the path does not. The repairs that guess intent stay withheld behind `.risky(true)`, and `risky_available` says how many were held back, so a caller can offer that choice instead of having to know the tier exists. `build` is the data door, where `write` is the document one: hand it `GroupData` rows and it produces AGS4, deriving the `UNIT`/`TYPE` catalogues and validating what it wrote. Cells are a first-party `Cell` enum rather than the emit engine's `serde_json::Value`, which is the facade's no-third-party-type rule doing real work here: it is also what preserves the typed formatting Python and Node get from an Arrow frame, so a number goes through its heading's declared AGS TYPE (`12.5` under `2DP` is written `12.50`) while a string is written verbatim. A row whose length does not match its headings is refused by name — the safe fix set pads short rows, so without that check a miscounted column would come back as a finding about the output instead of as the caller's mistake. Both doors share one call into the emit engine with `write` rather than a second copy of it.
- **The Rust crate compares and reconciles deliveries — `ags4::diff` and `ags4::merge`.** `diff` answers what changed between two submissions in *AGS terms*, not text terms: rows are matched by their group's dictionary KEY headings rather than by line order, so a re-sorted borehole list pairs each row with its own prior self, and cells are compared through their declared TYPE, so `1.0` → `1.00` is not a change. A line diff gets both wrong. `merge` reconciles N deliveries in order — a later file wins — with the same KEY-aware row identity, so a re-sorted delivery merges onto its prior self instead of doubling it, and every revision it makes is reported so the merge stays auditable. A column two producers typed differently is **refused by default**: resolving that is a judgement about their data, and `on_type_clash` offers the two honest answers — widen to free text (bytes untouched, type discarded) or promote to the greatest `nDP` precision (never the lowest, which would round data away). A column they gave different *units* is refused in every mode, because no resolution exists that does not silently mislabel one file's values. Those two failures now have their own `ErrorKind`s — `TypeConflict` and `UnitConflict`, carrying the same `type_conflict` / `unit_conflict` tokens the Python, Node and `lat` surfaces already use — rather than collapsing onto one, because they need different fixes. Both doors take a path, bytes, or a read handle; the handle form uses each document **as it stands, edits included**, since diffing the file it was read from would quietly ignore the edit.
- **`tests/test_docs_snippets.py` — the docs' hand-written Python is executed now.** `test_docs_examples.py` and `gen_doc_outputs.py --check` both key off the `--8<--` include, which covers 38 of the site's 60 Python fences; the other 22 are literal fragments, and together with `README.md`, the PyPI landing page and `COMPAT.md` nothing ran them (`--check-pages` inspects only *output* blocks, so a literal code fence is not even counted). The new gate treats a page as one program in document order — replaying includes so a fragment inherits the `ags`/`fixed` its page established — executes 85% of literal statements against the installed wheel and resolves names plus call keywords for the rest, with a coverage floor so it cannot decay into name-checking. It runs from a temp dir: these snippets write.
- **A docs Python example runs on its own — `uv run ex01_read_typed.py`, no clone.** Prototyped on one example ahead of the other 17. A PEP 723 `# /// script` header pins `requires-python` and an exact `laterite==`, and a fixture arm fetches `examples/sample_site.ags` when the repo-relative path is absent, so the code on the page stays the code you would type in a checkout instead of becoming an absolute path. Both sit above a `--8<-- [start:code]` marker and the page includes `…py:code`, so the rendered snippet is byte-identical to before — the CLI tree's `[start:cmd]` trick applied to Python. The arm is cold in CI, so no gate takes on a network dependency. The pin is a claim, so it is gated: `test_version_faithful.py` holds it and the interpreter floor to the shipped values by discovery, and `bump-version.sh` restamps it with a substitution anchored on `laterite==` — the sibling loop that stamps `.out` files rewrites every occurrence of the old version in a file, which is safe in generated output and would silently rewrite an `assert` in a source.
- **Every docs Python example now runs on its own — `uv run exNN_*.py`, no clone.** The prototype is rolled out to all 18 plus the marimo tour: a PEP 723 header pinning `requires-python` and an exact `laterite==`, a fixture arm fetching `examples/sample_site.ags` when the repo-relative path is absent, and a `--8<-- [start:code]` marker so the rendered page is byte-identical to before (asserted for all 18 against `git show HEAD:`). Two things the single-example prototype could not show: `ex09a`/`ex09b`/`ex15` build from frames, a typed graph and inline text, so they get no fixture arm — there is nothing to fetch for; and `ex05`/`ex11` import pandas, which is not in the base install, so they pin `laterite[compat]==`. A uniform bare pin makes both die under `uv run` on `ModuleNotFoundError: pandas`, verified. The README gains `uvx --from laterite lat validate delivery.ags` — a zero-install trial.
- **A nightly leg asks the reader's question: does the live docs site work against the wheel you can actually install?** Every existing docs gate runs against the working-tree cdylib, so all of them answer "is the site consistent with HEAD" — and the reader is not on HEAD, they are on `pip install laterite`. `docs-vs-released-wheel` installs the published wheel (unpinned, whatever PyPI resolves that day) and runs the examples plus `tests/test_docs_snippets.py` against it, printing the released version beside the tree's. The two steps are calibrated differently on purpose: an example that fails to RUN fails the job, because a reader following the site would get a traceback; a committed `.out` that no longer byte-matches is reported and not fatal, because output drift is the ordinary consequence of the tree being ahead. It stays out of `notify`'s `needs` for the same reason — the docs track HEAD by decision, so documenting unreleased API is a chosen state, and filing an issue about a chosen state is noise that gets muted.
- **Seven ungated output blocks are now generated, not hand-written.** `--check-pages` counts `text` fences no example backs; that count was 8 and is now 1. Four new CLI examples (clean-file `--json`, a one-value typo, and the warning/errors-only tier pair, the last three minting their input from the fixture with `sed` so CRLF survives) and two new Python examples close `learn/install.md`, `concepts/severity-tiers.md` and `concepts/one-engine-many-doors.md`. The remaining orphan is `chaining/index.md`'s ASCII flow diagram — a drawing, not the output of anything, so it stays unwired by design: the target is zero GATEABLE orphans, not zero orphans.
- **Every crate README example is now a doctest.** Three lines per crate — `#[cfg(doctest)] #[doc = include_str!("../README.md")] mod readme_doctests {}` — point rustdoc at the README, so `cargo test --workspace` compiles all ten (eight execute; two touch the filesystem and are `no_run`). No new CI, no duplication: the README stays the single copy, and `cfg(doctest)` keeps the module out of both a normal build and the docs.rs page, so the crates' own `//!` docs are untouched — verified by grepping the generated HTML. Each fence is written out in full because a README is also read as Markdown on crates.io, where rustdoc's `# ` hidden lines would render as headings. `tests/test_crate_readme_doctests.py` asserts the wiring by discovery, rejects an `ignore` fence, and fails a fence in a crate excluded from the CI doctest run — where it would look gated and be checked by nothing.
- **The Node docs' hand-typed JavaScript is executed now.** `docs-examples.test.ts` and `gen_doc_outputs --surface node` both key off the `--8<--` include, covering 18 fences; 11 more are typed straight into the Markdown and the npm landing page carries 4 — the page a reader sees before `npm install` — and none of it ran. `laterite-node/test/docs-snippets.test.ts` welds each page into one ESM program (imports unioned per module, re-declarations turned into assignment, since ESM forbids the rebind Python allows) and executes it from a temp cwd with the fixture copied in. All four pages run; a fence that genuinely cannot — the wasm type declarations, the `{ arrow: true }` call that downloads a DuckDB community extension at run time — carries a `doc-snippet: skip` marker with its reason.
- **`laterite-node/test/peer-range.test.ts` — the published peer range must admit the version we develop against.** Offline and registry-free: if the range you tell users to install disagrees with the version your own tests run against, it cannot be right. That single assertion would have caught the ETARGET above the day it was introduced.
- **`docs-vs-released-npm` — the Node twin of the released-wheel nightly.** Installs `laterite` from npm unpinned, then the optional peer exactly as the docs and the runtime error tell a reader to, then runs the docs examples against it. Same calibration as the wheel leg: an example that fails to RUN fails the job, an `.out` byte-mismatch is reported and not fatal, and it stays out of `notify`'s `needs`. Building this job is what surfaced the unsatisfiable `peerDependencies` range, so it had earned its keep before running once — and it will be red until that fix ships, which is the correct signal rather than a defect in the job.
- **`laterite.compat` mirrors python-ags4's module layout — `compat.AGS4`, `compat.check`, `compat.utils`, `compat.data`.** The drop-in was one flat module where upstream is a package, so `from python_ags4.AGS4 import AGS4Error` — third-party production code, not a hypothetical — had no laterite equivalent at all. The parity oracle could never have caught this: its shim aliases four distinct upstream modules to one object, so 121/131 green was a statement about flattened function behaviour and structurally blind to module boundaries. Every import shape a real python-ags4 user writes now ports by changing one token, `python_ags4` -> `laterite.compat`, and `tests/test_compat_import_shapes.py` holds that true by asserting placement rather than mere presence — a name drifting between submodules fails even though the flat namespace would still resolve it. The flat namespace is unchanged and remains the primary surface; the submodules re-export from it. `compat.check` also gains `STANDARD_DICT_FILES` and `LATEST_DICT_VERSION`, mirrored verbatim — the fallback is 4.1.1 rather than the newest key, because upstream ships a 4.2 dictionary and still defaults to 4.1.1 when TRAN_AGS is absent — and `compat.data` ships a sample file whose contents are clean-room (upstream's is LGPL-3.0). There is still no top-level `python_ags4` import name in the wheel, now stated as a permanent non-goal rather than an unrecorded gap: two distributions cannot both own `site-packages/python_ags4/`. Undocumented private helpers (`compat._try_dict_version` and friends) moved to `compat._impl` with the body.
- **ARM64 Linux is a shipped target again — `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`.** It joins `napi.targets`, the wheel matrix and the binaries matrix, so all three artifacts ship the same platform list. Its 2025 removal rested on a billing dependency on a then-private repo, and on a comment blaming a self-hosted pool `release.yml` never used; neither holds now and the runner is free. Platform parity keeps it honest: a triple shipped by one artifact is shipped by all.

### Changed

- **laterite is in beta.** One claim covering everything shipped, replacing four enumerations in the repo that disagreed about which surfaces exist. PyPI's `Development Status` classifier moves from `3 - Alpha` to `4 - Beta` — the only machine-readable status field the project owns; npm, crates.io and the web app have no equivalent field, so they carry the claim as a README line and a footer link instead of in a `description`, which is read while deciding whether to click and cannot carry the explanation that makes the claim fair. The Rust crate `laterite` is the one exception, and for completeness rather than quality: it is not yet at parity with the other five surfaces (`dec-facade-parity` phase 4 of 9) and joins when it is — it runs the same engine they do.
- **The Excel crate is `laterite-ags4-excel`.** It was `laterite-excel` — a name chosen for the general-purpose Excel library it was meant to become and never did. `-ags4-` marks the engine tier and bare `laterite-*` is for the format-agnostic crates, of which `laterite-transport` is the only genuine one; this crate holds contents its own header calls AGS4-specific. Renamed **now** because a crates.io name is free until its first publish and irreversible after, and this crate is scheduled to publish — the same reasoning that renamed `laterite-ags4-check` to `laterite-cli` before the engine tier went out. Nothing a user types changes: the Python, Node, browser and `lat excel` surfaces are untouched, and the crate has never been on a registry for anyone to depend on. Internally the lib name moves with it, so `laterite_excel::` becomes `laterite_ags4_excel::` at every call site. Past release entries here carry the new name too, deliberately: one grep gives one answer rather than an exception list to carry forward.
- **`tests/test_docs_node_api.py` now also scans the npm landing page.** Falsification of the new executor found the gap: a bare `report.someTypo` evaluates to `undefined` and logs rather than throwing, so executing cannot catch it, and the static gate scanned `docs/node/` only — leaving `laterite-node/README.md` covered by neither. The executor catches calls, the resolver catches reads; neither subsumes the other.
- **The compiled dependency set moves forward: arrow 59.1 → 59.2, PyO3 0.29.0 → 0.29.2, napi 3.12.0 → 3.12.1 (with `napi-derive` 3.6.1 → 3.6.3 and `napi-build` 2.4.0 → 2.4.1), `thiserror` 2.0.19 → 2.0.20 and `rust_xlsxwriter` 0.97.0 → 0.97.1.** Declared here rather than waved through because this repo ships BUILT artefacts — these are the versions actually inside the wheel, the Node addon, the wasm bundle and `lat`, not ranges a consumer's own resolver gets to pick from. All are patch or minor moves within the existing manifest ranges, so only `Cargo.lock` changes; no API a caller touches moves with them. The arrow bump was additionally checked against the co-residency fault fixed earlier in this cycle — `import pyarrow` then `import laterite`, with pyarrow 25.0.0, still hands back intact buffers under the mimalloc v2 pin.
- **Breaking: the Node package requires Node >= 22.** `engines` said `>=18` for fifteen months and was never true — an unverified guess rather than a support commitment, with nothing in CI testing Node 18 or 20. It now equals the tested floor, with Node 24 added to the matrix beside it. Done now rather than later because there is no user to break, and the cost of correcting the number will never be lower.
- **The compatibility promise now says which surface it is about.** "laterite is in beta, and pre-1.0 a minor may break you" and "this crate exists so that reshaping does not reach you" were both true, both shipped, and being printed apart — four lines from each other, about the same crate. They are one statement in two clauses now: the facade absorbs *engine* reshaping, and its own surface is pre-1.0 and may break you. The docs site's `reference/support.md` gains **How versions move**, which states the rule once for the three version lines actually running — the product line (one number, one changelog, minor-for-breaking, in beta), the Rust crate (its own clock, outside the beta claim, changes faster), and the engine crates (no promise at all: machinery, not a door). "Read the changelog before upgrading" is deliberately a product-line clause only, and names root `CHANGELOG.md`, where the breaking-changes index makes it a short list rather than a read; the Rust crate gets the honest form instead — the API will change, Cargo will not carry you across a `0.x` minor on a caret requirement, don't force one — because a Rust consumer is protected by the resolver whether they read anything or not, and `pip install laterite` unpinned is not. `reference/changelog.md` now leads with `CHANGELOG.md` instead of the GitHub Releases feed, which is the artifact with a drift gate behind it. ([#318](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/318))
- **The site has its own home: `laterite.dev`.** The browser validator answers at `app.laterite.dev` and the documentation at `docs.laterite.dev` — two hosts, where before they rode one artifact with the docs in a subdirectory of the app. Every published link moves with them. The old `niko86.github.io/laterite/` URLs keep working: that site stays up serving nothing but redirects, which is what makes the move safe after 0.8.x and 0.9.0 froze the old host into READMEs on PyPI, npm and crates.io that can never be edited. **If you allowlist hosts, add `cdn.laterite.dev`** — the DuckDB engine behind the Explore tab is a 34-39 MiB wasm and the static-asset host caps a single file at 25 MiB, so that one file is served from object storage on the same domain. Validate, Fix and the rest are unaffected, and nothing about the privacy claim changes: no file you open has ever left the browser and none does now. Two links were already dead and are fixed on the way past: the bug template pointed reporters at the known-divergences page and the issue chooser at the feedback page, both omitting the `/docs/` segment, so the first two links anybody filing a bug follows were 404s. Nothing checks a URL that lives in an issue template. ([#332](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/332))
- **Breaking: `@laterite/ags4-wasm` is the slim engine — 757 KiB gzipped instead of 1.8 MB.** One artifact used to carry everything, so a page that only wanted to validate a file still downloaded the Excel reader/writer, Arrow IPC, the certificate stack, diff, merge and censor. Six cargo features now gate those — `excel`, `arrow`, `certify`, `diff`, `merge`, `censor` — and the published package is built with none of them: 1.9 MB raw / 757 KiB gzip / 574 KiB brotli, against 6.4 MB / 1.8 MB / 1.3 MB for the full engine. **What leaves npm is `arrow_ipc` and `build_ags4_ipc`, `ags4_to_xlsx` and `xlsx_to_ags4`, `certify`, `diff`, `merge` and `censor`**; every one is still there in a source build, because `default = full` and the features are ON by default — the app at app.laterite.dev compiles the crate itself and is unaffected. The one place this bites a caller rather than merely removing a verb is `read`: the handle's rows came back as Arrow IPC and now come back as JSON from the new `rows_json()`, through the SAME `parse_value` cast — a `2DP` heading is still a number, a `DT` still a datetime string — so the values are identical and only the framing differs. It is not a drop-in for `arrow_ipc()`, which is why this declares itself breaking. Nothing was removed from the middle of the chain: read → validate → **fix** → write is intact, and `meta()` + `rows_json()` together are exactly `build_ags4`'s input shape, so a browser round-trip composes without an adapter. Gates rather than compiler flags because the measurement said so: our own Rust is ~7.6% of the binary and `arrow` alone ~35% of its code section, while every compiler knob tried came to ~180 KB between them — `opt-level = "z"` and `"s"` were both measured and both rejected, at 13–95% slower in the browser. A gate holds the split: `tools/release/check-wasm-slim.mjs` checks the exported surface exactly AND a gzip ceiling, and it gates on gzip rather than raw bytes because those two disagree — switching `diff` back on adds 1.47 MB raw but only 82 KB brotli, so a raw ceiling would fire on changes nobody downloads and stay quiet on ones they do.
- **The dictionary was embedded twice; now it is embedded once — 1.4 MB off every artifact.** `laterite-ags4-reference` compiles `ags_dictionary.json` into `phf` tables at build time, which is why the crate's own docs said it reads "nothing at runtime". Its `union` module did not: it carried a SECOND copy of the same 1.4 MB file via `include_str!` and parsed it on the first `registry()` call to rebuild the all-editions union. Every artifact that touched the registry paid for both — the browser wasm, the wheel's `.so`, `lat`, the Node addon. `union_groups()` now reconstructs that union from the masked tables instead (each group and heading at its newest edition, in `gen_dictionary.py`'s heading order), so nothing is stored twice: **wasm 6,722,493 → 5,312,456 raw (−21.0%)**, `lat` −18.7%, the Node addon −15.5%, the wheel's `.so` −7.1%. Behaviour is unchanged and that is asserted rather than asserted-about: the JSON stays as a `#[cfg(test)]` ORACLE, and a differential test compares the reconstruction against it across all 174 groups and ~3,500 headings — field by field, order included — because "spot-check PROJ and LOCA" would not notice a heading whose edition set moved its latest definition. It is a SIZE win and not a startup one: `union_groups()` went 2.13 ms → 1.56 ms, since both paths allocate the same owned headings and the parse was never the dominant cost. Worth saying how it hid for so long — JSON that repetitive compresses ~18:1, so the duplicate was 1.4 MB raw but only ~54 KB of what a browser actually downloads, and every compressed-size check reported it as fine. Raw size is what found it, which is the general lesson: the two axes disagree, and only one of them shows a redundant blob. A second test now fails the build if an `include_str!` of the dictionary reappears outside the oracle.

### Removed

- **`compat.AGS4_to_dataframe_AGS3`, which mirrored nothing.** `git log -S` over python-ags4's entire history shows no such function has ever existed, in any version — so the stub was a laterite invention, and COMPAT.md's API table listed it as mirroring an upstream function in order to claim a divergence against it. AGS3 is out of scope for this project. The real O-30 refusal is unaffected: it happens on the ordinary entry points, exactly as upstream aborts on its own AGS3 detection, and is now tested there with real AGS3-shaped input instead of through a function nobody could have called.

### Fixed

- **The wheel could corrupt pyarrow's memory just by being imported.** `import pyarrow` followed by `import laterite` was enough to leave a subsequently-built `pyarrow.Table` holding zeroed bytes — no laterite call on the path, and no Arrow FFI involved. The damage was silent until some later native call tripped over it, so for months it surfaced as an intermittent SIGSEGV blamed on whichever innocent test ran next, never on the thing that caused it. pyarrow bundles its own mimalloc as its default memory pool and the `mimalloc` crate defaults to v3, and two co-resident v3 instances hand out overlapping memory (microsoft/mimalloc#1327; apache/arrow GH-50428 is the same fault from Arrow's side — a pyarrow 24.0.0 regression fixed in 25.0.1, whose own recommended workaround is the pin taken here). All three native surfaces — the wheel, the Node addon and `lat` — now pin mimalloc v2. Only pyarrow-bearing installs were ever affected (`[pyarrow]`, `[compat,pyarrow]`, `[all]`); polars and duckdb are unaffected, so the base install was never exposed. Keeping the allocator was the point: v2 holds ~18-19% read and ~14-15% validate over the system allocator, which dropping mimalloc would have given back.
- **`COMPAT.md` documented a `check_file` keyword that has never existed, and a version frozen nine releases back.** Both blocks of the error-handling section passed `dictionary='not-a-dict.txt'`; the parameter is `standard_AGS4_dictionary` in laterite *and* in python-ags4, so the two snippets illustrating the divergence raised `TypeError` on both sides and showed the reader nothing — the prose was correct, only the code was uncopyable. The `laterite.compat.__version__` doctest, the `Metadata.Checker` banner a user sees in their own validation report, and the phase-1 illustration all still said `0.1.0`. `bump-my-version` stamps those two strings in `compat.py` and had no `COMPAT.md` entry, so code and page provably diverged on every release; neither superseded-version gate could catch it, because both match versions listed in `changelog.json` and its history starts at 0.6.0. The page is now stamped, and `tests/test_docs_snippets.py` asserts it against the wheel's real values.
- **`gen_doc_outputs.py` silently under-counted a page that included an example SECTION.** The include→example map registered the literal `:cmd` spelling beside the bare filename, so the first page to use any other section name fell through the `not in wanted` branch as "a surface this run didn't ask for" — pointing three pages at `…py:code` dropped the matched-block count from 38 to 35 and still reported success. The key is now the include with its section suffix stripped, which covers every section name there will ever be.
- **The PEP 723 pin gate could not see the file that motivated it.** It matched `laterite==(version)` and compared the version, which passes anything that is not an exact pin at all — so `examples/laterite_tour.py` asking for `laterite>=0.5.0` at product 0.10.1 (five minors of compatibility it claimed and nobody had tested) produced no match and therefore no finding, and a bare `"laterite"` escaped identically. The gate now asserts the whole specifier, discovers across both example trees rather than the docs corpus alone, and admits the `[extras]` group that the pandas examples need — `bump-version.sh` was equally blind to `laterite[compat]==`, which would have frozen those two pins at the old version while every sibling moved.
- **`learn/install.md` printed its findings table in the wrong renderer.** The first page a new user reads showed plain ASCII pipes (`Rule | Line | Group`) — what the wheel's Python `lat` console script renders — on a page documenting the Rust binary, which draws comfy-table box-drawing. The row's content was correct, so somebody ran it once and nothing re-ran it: exactly the drift the CLI example gate was built for, in the blocks that gate never covered because no example backed them.
- **Three crates.io READMEs documented Rust that does not compile.** `laterite-ags4-parse` iterated `parsed.groups` — a `BTreeMap` — as though it were a sequence, so `group.code` was a field access on a `(&String, &ParsedGroup)` tuple; `laterite-ags4-core` called `read_ags4_bytes(&bytes, opts)`, which takes one argument (the two-argument form is `read_ags4_bytes_with`); and `laterite-transport` called `lock(src, dest, pw, level)`, which takes five — the scrypt `log_n` was missing. A published version's README is frozen on crates.io, and `check_doc_refs.py` already treated those pages as a strict special case for their links; their code was checked by nothing.
- **`node/index.md` documented `buildAgs4` with an input it rejects.** The page showed `buildAgs4({ PROJ: [{ PROJ_ID: "P1" }] })`; the signature is `AgsGroup | Map<string, GroupData> | Array<[string, GroupData]>`, so a reader copying it got `TypeError: items is not iterable`. Confirmed against the built package before fixing, and the page now shows a `Map` with a note that a plain object is not one of the accepted shapes.
- **`sql()` and `at()` were unreachable for anyone installing the npm package.** `peerDependencies: { "@duckdb/node-api": ">=1.5.0" }` matched ZERO of that package's 56 published versions: every release carries a prerelease suffix (`1.5.5-r.3`, …), and semver excludes a prerelease from a range unless a comparator shares its major.minor.patch AND carries a prerelease itself — so `>=1.5.0` matched nothing, and neither did `>=1.5.0-0` or even `*`. All three install orders were reproduced against the published package: `npm i laterite` then `npm i @duckdb/node-api` (the exact command the library's own error text prints) fails with ETARGET; installing both in one command drops the peer silently; installing the peer first has it actively removed when laterite arrives. The range is now `>=1.5.5-0`, the devDependency is aligned to the same line, and the documented flow was verified end to end — install resolution against a packed build, and `sql()`/`at()` actually running against the published one. No existing gate could see this: `npm ci` installs from the lockfile, so the peer range is never consulted.
- **The docs quoted a `compat` speedup lower than the one the benchmark measures.** Three docs-site pages and the wheel's own `pyproject.toml` comment said `laterite.compat` runs “~2× faster than python-ags4”. The published table in the wheel README measures 2.9×, 3.5×, 3.2×, 3.3× and 3.3× across its five file sizes — every rung above 2.9, so the prose understated the product on all of them, on the first page a python-ags4 user reads. The two figures were never the same measurement: the `~2×` dates from the 2026-07-20 Arrow pass and comes from a bench whose fixture is three data groups, where the README table is the same public call across five sizes of a 123-group scaffold. Reader-facing text now takes the published figure; the two wiki pages still carrying the old number name the fixture it belongs to instead of having a digit swapped under them, because a measurement nobody re-ran must not be quietly restated as a different one. Nothing ties prose to that table, which is why it drifted for a month — tracked as [#327](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/issues/327). ([#326](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/326))
- **The published list of python-ags4 divergences is generated now, and it had been wrong in five places.** `reference/divergences.md` is the page an evaluating reader meets, and it was hand-written against `observations.json` — a source of truth that is generated and gated everywhere else in the repo. It told readers the external `--dict` override “is deferred” a release after #568 shipped it; four more rows carried supersession the page did not reflect; and it had never gained O-49 or O-50. It is rendered from the catalogue now, with the same drift gate the rest of that render already had. Two things changed for a reader beyond the corrections: the headline count is computed rather than asserted (**17** records change what you see, where the page claimed 19 and neither number was checkable), and the page groups by what actually happened instead of filing everything under “Known divergences from python-ags4” — a title that was wrong about four of its own rows, since O-1 and O-32 are cases where laterite *matches* python-ags4 and both depart from the spec, and O-31 and O-33 are laterite's own false negatives that the comparison caught and closed. ([#320](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/issues/320))

## [0.10.1] — 2026-08-04

### Added

- **The browser package has an API reference.** `@laterite/ags4-wasm` ships to npm with fully typed results, and until now the docs site did not mention it once — the crate README was its only documentation. `reference/wasm-api.md` documents it through the practices the web app actually uses, with worked examples whose printed output is generated from running them: init once and await that promise (and pass `module_or_path` explicitly, or a non-root `base` breaks the fetch fallback), read severity through one resolver because an absent `severity` means *error*, take the types from the package rather than mirroring them, hold a `ParsedDataset` across its Arrow pulls and free it before the next parse, propose fixes before applying them, and keep the synchronous engine off the main thread.
- **`laterite.dev` answers.** A deliberately thin placeholder — what the project is, and the three links that matter (the browser app, the docs, the source). It exists now because the apex was being *advertised* while serving nothing: the redirect shim left on the old GitHub Pages host names `laterite.dev` in its canonical tag and its no-JavaScript fallback, so every crawler following it, and every visitor without JavaScript, was pointed at a hostname with no record. A redirect rule would have closed that too; a Worker was chosen because the real landing page will be one, so this is the same object thinner rather than scaffolding to remove later.

### Changed

- **The `lat` console script the wheel installs now renders the same tables as the shipped `lat` binary.** Two programs answer to `lat` — the Rust binary and this Python console script — and until now they printed visibly different output for the same command: comfy-table's UTF-8 box grid from one, a plain `ljust` grid from the other. The machine-readable surfaces (`--json`, `--ndjson`, `--csv`, the group listing, exit codes) had always been held byte-identical by test; the grids people actually read were pinned nowhere, which is how the divergence survived. The glyphs are now matched exactly, colour included (bold-cyan header, dim alternate rows, honouring `NO_COLOR` and a real terminal the same way the binary does), and the human table has joined the byte-parity tests instead of being excluded from them. **No new dependency:** the CLI remains stdlib-only. The two still part under an interactive TTY, where comfy-table wraps to the terminal width and this does not — a case no gate or document captures.
- **The browser story is one page instead of thirteen near-identical tabs.** Each cookbook page carried a *Browser* tab saying the same three sentences — same engine, in your browser, nothing uploaded — about whichever pane of the web app was relevant. Those are consolidated into the web app's own page (`surfaces/browser.md`), which now describes what each pane gives you; the cookbook's *Available in* line links there instead. The app is a showcase for the wasm package, not a product, so it gets one page describing it and the package gets the API reference every other surface already had.
- **The web app lints on ESLint 10.** It was the last surface still on 9 — `laterite-node` had already moved — and the bump was blocked by `eslint-plugin-solid`, whose peer range stops at `^9.0.0` and whose last release was December 2024. That peer is now relaxed by an `overrides` entry, which is only defensible because the thing an override can hide was checked: the plugin's rules still **fire** under 10 (a deliberate `solid/reactivity` violation is still caught), not merely load. Two of 10's new rules earned the upgrade. `preserve-caught-error` found a real defect in the wasm-tokenizer test setup, which interpolated the caught error's `.message` into a new one and dropped the original — throwing away the stack that distinguishes *nobody ran the build* from *the wasm will not instantiate*, the one moment you need to tell them apart; it now attaches `cause`. `no-unassigned-vars` flagged four Solid ref bindings, where the JSX compiler does the write the rule cannot see (and the definite-assignment `!` does not satisfy it — three of the four already carried one); it is off for `.tsx` only, so a never-assigned `let` in a plain `.ts` module stays a hard failure.
- **A narrowed `AGS4_to_dataframe` no longer builds the groups it is about to throw away.** `only_groups` narrowed the *result*, but the narrowing happened in Python — the native parse had already built and crossed an Arrow table for every group in the file, and the unwanted ones were constructed, handed over the PyO3 boundary and discarded. The narrowing is now pushed down into the parse itself: asking for one group of 123 on a 25 MB file takes **131.2 ms instead of 144.4 ms (−9.1%)**, and the ~25 MB of Arrow tables nobody asked for is never allocated. A full read (`only_groups=None`, the default every existing caller takes) builds every group exactly as before. What it deliberately does **not** narrow is python-ags4's three hard raises — duplicate GROUP, ragged DATA row, and duplicate heading under `rename_duplicate_headers=False` — which read the whole file and still fire on an offence in a group the caller filtered out. Narrowing those too would turn a rejected file into an accepted one, so every group still carries its headings, line anchors and ragged list; only the table is conditional.
- **The npm package's native loader reports a failed load properly, and understands `NAPI_RS_WASI_FLAVOR`.** `index.js` is generated by `@napi-rs/cli`, so a toolchain bump (3.7.4 → 3.8.2) rewrites it — and this one is not cosmetic. A load failure used to surface as whichever single error came last; it now builds a chain, each `Error` carrying the previous one as its `cause`, so "the addon would not load" finally tells you *which* of the candidate binaries failed and why. The WASI fallback also gained a flavour selector: `NAPI_RS_WASI_FLAVOR` picks a specific build and rejects an unknown value by name rather than silently ignoring it, and setting it now implies forcing WASI. Nothing in the loader's happy path changed — a successful `require('laterite')` resolves exactly as before.
- **The bundled dictionary is stored once, not five times.** The five AGS4 editions overlap almost entirely — 89% of heading keys carry an identical definition in every edition they appear in — but the compiled tables held a complete copy per edition. They are now one set of tables keyed by the union, each key carrying one variant per *distinct* value plus a bitmask of the editions holding it. Nothing a consumer can observe changes: `dict_projection_pin` hashes every observable of every edition and reproduces all five digests exactly, which is why that test was written before the repack rather than after. Generated source drops 2,783,973 -> 906,008 bytes (-67%); the browser wasm drops 6.4% raw and 4.2% gzipped, which is 82 KiB off a gzipped payload. The gap between those two figures is the linker already deduplicating repeated string literals — what the repack removes is five copies of the table *structure*, not five copies of the strings.

### Fixed

- **28 of the docs site's 30 admonitions rendered as an empty box.** Prettier de-indents the body of a `!!! note` / `??? tip`, and MkDocs needs that indentation to associate the body with the box — so the text escaped into a plain paragraph underneath while the titled box rendered empty. Because `prettier --check` is a CI gate, writing an admonition *correctly* meant failing the gate, which is why only two survived. The docs' Markdown is now outside prettier's scope (it is MkDocs-flavoured — admonitions, content tabs and `--8<--` includes are not prettier's dialect) and every body is re-indented; the built site now has zero empty admonition boxes.
- **The release advisor recommended the wrong bump, in two different ways.** `gen_changelog.py --advise` is what `RELEASING.md` sends you to before stamping a version, and it disagreed with the policy paragraph in that same document. First, the pre-1.0 rule was applied in one place and not the other: `_bump()` correctly refused MAJOR at `0.x`, but the other branch escalated any non-empty `added` to MINOR regardless of version — so a documentation page would have cut a minor, which pre-1.0 *means* "something broke". Second, and worse, whether a change was breaking was decided by searching the entry prose for `\bbreaking\b`, which cannot tell a marker from a sentence denying one: "a non-breaking change" matched (the hyphen is a word boundary), as did "this is not a breaking change" and "avoids breaking downstream consumers". Every historical hit was a true positive only because the house style happened to be disciplined. Compatibility is now **declared** — `"breaking": true` on the entry — and the prose marker is kept as a cross-check the generator enforces in every mode: flag without marker, or marker without flag, fails. The six historical breaking entries are backfilled. The stakes are why: the engine tier publishes to crates.io, where a version can never be re-cut.

## [0.10.0] — 2026-08-02

The Rust engine has an audience it did not have before: eight crates are on crates.io, and `laterite` is a real Rust API rather than a reserved name. That brought a second version number with it — the engine answers to `cargo add`, the products to `pip install` and `npm i` — so every surface now reports which ENGINE it carries, and the cross-surface gate checks it was comparing one. **Breaking:** the browser package finishes what 0.9.0 started — `diff` and `censor` take an options object like every other export, and `any` is gone from the `.d.ts` entirely.

### Added

- **The browser package publishes its remaining result types, and `any` is gone from its `.d.ts` entirely.** `diff`, `dictionary` and `compute_fixes` were the three still returning `any`; they now return `RevisionDelta`, `StandardDict` and `Fix[]`, joining the shapes published previously. Consumers can delete their hand-written `RevisionDelta` / `StandardDict` / `Fix` / `SpanEdit` / `CellDelta` / `RowDelta` / `GroupDelta` / `DictGroup` / `DictHeading` mirrors — the validator site deleted ~120 lines of exactly those. Each new interface is bound to the Rust struct that serialises it by the same drift test as the others, and `Fix`'s `kind`/`risk` unions are checked against the validator's own enums, so a new fix kind cannot ship a `.d.ts` that lies about what you can receive. ([#188](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/188))
- **The fingerprint build refuses to emit a digest that covers too little.** It previously narrowed in silence — the dependency walk simply found nothing and carried on. It now fails the build, naming what it found. The existing coverage test cannot do this job: tests do not ship in a published crate, so the one build that had the defect was also the one build with nothing checking it. ([#190](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/190))
- **Three gates that have to work before the first crates.io publish, not after.** A published version's public API and its declared `rust-version` are both frozen, and the only remedy for either being wrong is a version bump every consumer has to follow. The new `publish-gates` CI job (1) builds the ten engine crates on the `rust-version` their own manifests declare, (2) diffs each crate's rendered public API against a checked-in snapshot under `tools/release/public-api/`, and (3) runs `cargo semver-checks` against `main`. The snapshot is the one that changes review: it puts the whole public surface into the PR's own diff, including the `Send`/`Sync` impls that are public API nobody writes down — an `Rc` in a private field silently removes `Send` from a consumer's type, and that is now a build failure rather than something a reviewer has to notice. Opaque `-> impl Trait` returns are the one thing a snapshot cannot see, so each is asserted at compile time instead, and the gate refuses to let a new one be added without one. ([#193](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/193))
- **The engine crates carry the metadata a crates.io page is made of.** `repository`, `keywords` and `categories` were absent, and seven of the eight round-one crates had no README. That is not a cosmetic gap: crates.io bakes metadata into the PUBLISHED VERSION, so adding it afterwards fixes future versions only — the pages for a version already on the registry would keep no link back to the source, permanently, and seven of them would have been a one-line description and nothing else. Each README is written to stand alone on the registry rather than assume the repository around it. The packaging gate caught all seven new files, which is what it is for. ([#195](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/195))
- **The eight round-one engine crates are armed for crates.io, and there is a tool that publishes them safely.** Every crate carried `publish = false` — a blanket safety catch, so `cargo publish` refused outright. It is now `true` on the eight; `laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` stay `false`, held for 0.2, with the reason recorded at the flag rather than somewhere a reader has to go looking. `tools/publish_crates.py` does the release: it derives the dependency waves from the manifests each run rather than restating them, waits for each wave to become RESOLVABLE from the registry (not merely uploaded — crates.io indexes on a delay, and a plain loop dies on wave 2 with wave 1 already permanently published), and is idempotent, so a re-run after a failure resumes instead of restarting. It refuses a dirty tree, any branch but `main`, a HEAD that is not `origin/main`, and any crate still marked `publish = false`. Nothing happens without `--execute`. ([#196](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/196))
- **The engine crates are on crates.io.** Eight of them at 0.9.0 — `laterite-ags4-parse`, `-types`, `-reference`, `-core`, `-validator`, `-emit`, `-trust` and `laterite-transport` — so a Rust consumer no longer needs a git dependency or a vendored path. `laterite-ags4-diff` and `laterite-ags4-merge` are deliberately NOT published; they ship in 0.2, and the `publish = false` guard is what keeps that a decision rather than something to remember. `tools/publish_crates.py` gained `--through-wave N`, so a release can publish one wave, let the live pages be inspected, and only then commit the rest — worth the pause while metadata is still correctable on the crates that have not gone out. ([#197](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/197))
- **`laterite` — a Rust API, not just a facade.** The user-facing crate now exists and is functional at 0.1.0: read an AGS4 file from a path or bytes, walk its groups/headings/rows, edit cells and append rows, validate against the full numbered rule set, and write valid AGS4 back out. It carries its own version, deliberately — the engine crates are lockstep 0.9.x and reshape as the format work demands; this one is a different promise to a different audience. The design's central rule is now **mechanically enforced** rather than reviewed for: no third-party type may appear anywhere in its public API, checked against the rendered surface, so a `serde_json::Value` return or an `encoding_rs::Encoding` argument fails the build instead of silently binding our semver to a dependency's. `encoding_rs` is not even a dependency — encodings are WHATWG label strings. Held for 0.2, additively: diff, merge, typed cell access, indexed scan. ([#198](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/198))
- **`laterite` can validate bytes — `ags4::validate_bytes`, in 0.1.1.** 0.1.0 shipped `validate` taking a path only, which meant a service validating an upload had to give it a disk to sit on first. The reason written at the function — that Rule 20 is about files beside the `.ags`, so bytes could only answer half of it — did not hold: Rule 20 has been two modules since 2026-07-14, and `WorldScope` exists precisely to say which half ran, refusing the request with `WorldCheckRequiresSource` rather than reporting a clean Rule 20 nobody checked. Python, Node, wasm and the emitter were all already using it; the facade was the only surface that could not, and its error mapping already handled the token it never produced. Both arms now end at the engine's single door, so the edition resolved from `TRAN_AGS` and the 4.0.3→4.0.4 content guard cannot come out differently for one file read two ways — a test asserts exactly that, since it is the bug every hand-assembled surface has had. Asking for the on-disk check on bytes is an error, not a pass. ([#200](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/200))
- **Every surface can say which ENGINE it carries, not just which release it is.** `engine_fingerprint()` and `engine_version()` now exist on the wheel (`laterite.engine_fingerprint()`), the npm package (`engineFingerprint()`) and the browser build. The fingerprint is a build-time digest over every rule source, the dictionary and the rules catalogue, so it is the only value that can be believed: edit a rule and forget to bump anything and the semver is unchanged while the digest moves. Two surfaces reporting the same fingerprint ARE running the same rules; two reporting the same release number merely shipped together — a distinction this repo has already been burned by, when a compliance report hard-coded a version literal and kept printing it two minors after the workspace moved past it. It is also what an `.ags.idx` certificate stamps, so it is the right thing to quote in a bug report. ([#203](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/203))
- **The cross-surface gate now checks it was comparing the same engine.** `xcheck` holds eight surfaces to the in-process Rust authority's bytes, and half of those legs run against BUILT ARTEFACTS — a `wasm-pack` output, a tsup dist, an installed wheel — any of which can be stale while every case still matches, because a stale engine and a current one usually agree. The run then reports N-way identity across a surface compiled two weeks ago. Each leg now reports the engine fingerprint it is ACTUALLY running, asked of the artefact rather than assumed from the tree, and a mismatch against the authority's is a hard failure that the allowlist cannot excuse — an allowlisted engine split would be the gate agreeing to compare two different engines, which is the one thing it exists to refuse. A version number could not have done this job; the digest moves when a rule is edited even if nobody bumps anything. The three `cli-*` launcher legs have no door to ask through yet, so they are NAMED on stderr as unchecked rather than passed over, and the run reads as five identity-checked surfaces plus a known gap instead of a clean bill of health. ([#204](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/204))
- **All eight cross-surface legs now prove they were running the same engine — the three `lat` launchers included.** #204 gave five of them a fingerprint to compare and left `cli-native`, `cli-uvx` and `cli-npx` naming themselves as unchecked, because a launcher is a subprocess and none of the three would say what engine it carried. They say it now, through `lat census` — the hidden machine dump all three already implement and `tools/gen_census.py` already diffs them across. A second machine door would have been a second thing to keep in step, which is the failure the census exists to catch. `engine` is deliberately NOT a census table and is absent from `surface-census.json`: a fingerprint moves whenever a rule is edited, so snapshotting it would churn a checked-in file on every rule change while saying nothing about the surfaces. The schema version still bumped, because a launcher built before the field answers with it MISSING and missing is indistinguishable from a launcher with nothing to report — it would opt itself out of the identity check in silence. That version is hand-declared in four places and nothing had ever pinned them equal; a test now does, since a bump that reaches three of four makes the fourth launcher permanently "stale" to the generator, which reads as a build problem rather than the typo it is. ([#205](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/205))
- **A surface that stops reporting its engine now fails CI instead of printing a warning above a green run.** The cross-surface gate gained a second anti-rot switch, `--require-engines all`, alongside the `--require-legs all` it has always had — and for the same reason: the same silence means different things locally and on a runner. On your machine a leg that cannot name its engine is a fact about your working tree; in CI it means a surface dropped out of the identity check while the gate still said OK, which is the exact shape of a gate disarming itself. The nightly job now passes both. Neither `engine-mismatch` nor `engine-unreported` can be allowlisted — there is no finding to triage, because the comparison an entry would excuse did not happen between the things it claims — and adding an entry does not merely fail to help: the run then fails **twice**, because the entry also trips the allowlist's own staleness check. ([#206](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/206))
- **The npm package's error-mapping table is tested, and its coverage floors moved 93/84 → 97/89.** `errors.ts` is the module that turns an engine failure into the class callers branch on (`instanceof FileNotFoundError`, not a message match) — and nothing tested it; it was covered only incidentally by suites that happened to trip some of its arms. The new suite reads the error kinds OUT OF THE RUST SOURCE rather than restating them, because a third hand-list is the failure this repo keeps paying for: `ValidatorError::kind()` calls itself the single producer of that value domain and a new variant does force its Rust match, but nothing forced `makeError` to keep up — an unmapped kind falls through to a base `Ags4Error` with the right message and the right exit code, so every `instanceof` a caller wrote silently becomes false. Also covered: the four source shapes a handle can re-read (a path is re-read from DISK, not snapshotted, so certifying after an edit measures the current file), `certify`'s refusal to overwrite a file that is not a certificate, and the guards on `diff`/`fix`/`buildAgs4` that turn a mistake into a typed error instead of a raw `ENOENT` or a lookup on `undefined`. ([#208](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/208))
- **The browser bundle's least-tested module was the one standing between DuckDB values and the DOM.** `duckTypes.ts` calls itself "the single audited place" where an Int64 column's `bigint` and a TIMESTAMP's micros-since-epoch are normalised — rendering a bigint in JSX throws, and a micros value read as millis renders a plausible date in 1970 rather than an error — and it sat at 15% of lines. It now has a suite, as does `loadSensitive()` (whose fetch-once cache and non-OK-response guard decide whether the Anonymiser pre-ticks anything at all: a proxy's JSON error page would otherwise yield a document with no headings, and an anonymiser that redacts nothing while looking like it worked). The parent-chain walkers in `relationships.ts` gained tests for their cycle guards, which existed to stop a malformed dictionary freezing the tab and had never been exercised. The web lane also gained a BRANCH floor, which it never had — that absence is why the badge read ~85% while the lines gate sat green above 95, since a half-taken branch counts as a hit to lcov and a partial to Codecov. Generated wasm-pack glue is now excluded from the denominator so a local run and the CI run measure the same thing. ([#209](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/209))
- **The browser engine has a coverage figure for the first time — it was 69%, and nobody could see it.** `laterite-ags4-wasm` was the one shipped surface with no coverage gate of any kind. The nightly Rust job excludes it, correctly, because folding a binding cdylib into the ENGINE's denominator would move the engine's floor for reasons unrelated to the engine — but the exclusion read as "cannot be measured", and so nothing ever measured it. It was never unmeasurable: its 44 tests are plain `#[test]`s that `cargo test` runs on every PR. It now has its own nightly step, its own denominator and its own floor, deliberately separate so the engine's floor stays comparable run-to-run. Four exports whose signatures are plain Rust — `version`, `engine_version`, `engine_fingerprint`, `list_rules` — gained native tests; the two identity doors especially, since `engine_fingerprint` exists because a hard-coded constant once stood in for a real answer here, and a constant is exactly what these would silently become again. The ceiling is now stated rather than discovered: 103 of 218 functions are unreachable from a native test because they take or return JS types, so raising this means moving logic out of the fat `#[wasm_bindgen]` exports into plain functions, not writing more tests against the boundary. ([#210](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/210))
- **The npm surface reaches the 95% coverage bar, and its floors move 97/89 → 98/91.** Five suites, each aimed at a decision that fails *quietly*. The `0DP` → `BIGINT` arm of the AGS-type mapping had never been exercised — a count that arrives as `7.0` is a different fact from `7`, and it round-trips back out that way. `_filteredRows`' `WHERE TRUE` fallback and the `* EXCLUDE (_id, _parent_id)` choice both produce a query that *runs*, with the wrong rows or the wrong columns. And `ancestorChain`/`inheritedKeyNames` translate a native throw as `e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`, where only the first arm was ever taken: napi can surface a non-`Error`, and without the second arm the `Ags4Error` reports the string `"undefined"` — the only diagnostic the caller had, gone. `registry.ts` goes 50 → 100% branch. Falsified by mutation rather than by assertion count: censor's default inverted, the `TRUE`/`FALSE` clause flipped, the null-fill removed and the `String(e)` arm removed are all caught. ([#214](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/214))
- **The browser bundle reaches 97.5% coverage — lines and functions both at 100% — and its branch floor moves 89 → 95.** Four suites, all aimed at code whose failure is a wrong *answer* rather than an error. An unqualified column in a join is ambiguous exactly when both sides carry the same heading, which for `LOCA_ID` is the *normal* case, and DuckDB resolves it by picking one; the Explore tab's suggested queries (`joinKeys`, `depthRangeOf`, `geologyTemplate`) run perfectly well while returning the wrong rows; and the union-dictionary fetch must throw on a non-OK response, because parsing a proxy's JSON error page instead yields a dictionary with no groups — an Explore tab where nothing is a known AGS group and nothing says why. `project()`'s output guard is now pinned against the official OS test points: `1e300` is finite, walks past the input check, and comes back unplottable. Falsified by mutation: the sensitive-policy guard dropped, the `!res.ok` throw removed, chart columns never alias-qualified, the `MC` gloss deleted and the template's depth check forced true are all caught. With the npm lane, this closes the last two lanes of the coverage campaign. ([#215](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/215))

### Changed

- **Breaking: `diff` and `censor` take an options object too.** They were the last two `@laterite/ags4-wasm` exports with a positional tail — `diff(a, b, encoding, maxRowsPerGroup)` and `censor(data, sensitiveJson, selectedCodes, token, dropCustom, includeFreetext)`, the latter six-deep with three consecutive booleans. Both now take one named object after their inputs (`diff(a, b, { encoding, maxRowsPerGroup })`, `censor(data, sensitiveJson, { selectedCodes, token, dropCustom, includeFreetext })`), every field optional and defaulted, with the same unknown-key refusal the other exports got. The test that recorded these two as "not yet migrated" now has nothing left to exempt. ([#188](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/188))
- **Every engine crate now declares what it may publish.** `cargo package` ships whatever sits in a crate directory and is not excluded, and no crate here specified `include` — `laterite-ags4-validator` alone would have put 41 test and bench files plus 2.1 MB of reference data no code reads into its tarball. All ten engine-tier crates now carry an explicit allowlist, and a CI gate diffs `cargo package --list` against a checked-in manifest so a new file entering a tarball turns the build red. This had to land before the first publish rather than after: crates.io is append-only, and `yank` stops new resolution without removing the tarball. ([#189](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/189))
- **The engine crates declare the versions a publish needs.** `cargo package` rejects a dependency with no version requirement — publishing strips the `path` and the version is all that survives to identify it — so 7 of the 10 engine-tier crates could not be packaged at all. The 21 in-workspace dependency sites now inherit from `[workspace.dependencies]`, which carries both a path and a version. Nothing changes locally: the path still wins, and `Cargo.lock` is untouched. The versions sit in `rust-packages/Cargo.toml` specifically so the release bump rewrites them alongside the workspace version rather than leaving them behind, and a test asserts that lockstep instead of assuming it. ([#191](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/191))
- **The CLI crate is `laterite-cli`.** `laterite-ags4-check` named a checker; the crate reads, fixes, diffs, merges, certifies, packs, converts and mints certificates, and `-ags4-` marks the engine tier, which a product binary is not. The shipped binary is still `lat` — nothing a user types changes. Renamed now because crates.io has no rename: a name is free until its first publish and irreversible after, and the engine tier went out yesterday. It is deliberately NOT added to the publish set, which looks like an oversight and is not: a binary's dependencies are still dependencies, so publishing it requires `laterite-ags4-diff` and `-merge` (held for 0.2) plus `laterite-cliutil` and `laterite-ags4-excel` (never considered for the registry) — and both publish gates render a lib target that a bin-only crate does not have. The CLI ships with 0.2, alongside the diff/merge publish it already depends on. ([#199](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/199))
- **There are two version numbers now: the engine and the products.** One number used to stamp the wheel, the npm package, the compat prefix and the Rust workspace together, and that coupling has a cost recorded in this repo's own history: `laterite-ags4-wasm` inherits the workspace version, so shipping a browser-only patch meant bumping the number every surface shared. It happened at 0.8.1 and again at 0.8.2, and because the release advice was "tag only what changed", PyPI saw neither — wheel versions 0.8.1 and 0.8.2 exist in git history and on no registry. Since the first crates.io publish there is a second cost: `[workspace.dependencies]` carries the version a published crate declares on its siblings, so bumping the engine for a product's sake would declare dependencies on engine versions nobody published. The engine (the Rust workspace and the eight crates.io crates) now moves on `bump-version.sh engine`; every product still shares one number and moves on `bump-version.sh product`. The target is required — a default would be a way to bump the wrong tier by omission. `laterite-cli` moved onto the product number, because `lat` exists twice and clap renders `--version` from `CARGO_PKG_VERSION`, so the binary and the wheel's `lat` would otherwise disagree the first time the tiers diverged. The gate asserts each tier is internally consistent and that the two stamping paths are disjoint, since an entry in the wrong config would silently restore the lockstep and look correct today, while the numbers are still equal. ([#202](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/202))
- **The browser engine's coverage went 69% → 91%, and it has a badge like every other language.** #210 stated the ceiling; this removes it. Fourteen `#[wasm_bindgen]` exports gave up their bodies to a host-testable `*_core` twin — `build_ags4`, `build_ags4_ipc`, `compute_fixes`, `apply_fixes`, `read`, `ParsedDataset.meta`/`arrow_ipc`, `diff`, `merge`, `dictionary`, `censor`, `ags4_to_xlsx`, `xlsx_to_ags4` — leaving `decode → core → marshal` at the boundary. That boundary is the floor of this measurement, not a backlog item: covering it needs `wasm-bindgen-test` on wasm32, which llvm-cov cannot instrument, so those tests would not move the number even once written; it is exercised end-to-end by the `wasm-engine` xcheck leg and the web content-hash test against the real `.wasm` instead. **No export changed behaviour** — including the two build doors' serializer, which writes `undefined` for an absent `line` where every other door writes `null`, preserved as released API and documented rather than quietly unified. 85 new tests, each falsified against a deliberate mutation of the code it guards. The floor moves 67 → 89, and `codecov.yml` stops documenting four floors that had all moved on without it. ([#211](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/211))

### Removed

- **`GroupDescriptor::table()` / `view()` are gone** (again). The two DuckDB `g_<code>`/`v_<code>` name builders sat on the format-neutral reference-data leaf with no callers but their own unit test, and publishing that crate would have frozen an unrelated product's schema naming into its public API. They were deleted in #175 — but #178 branched before it and squash-merged after, so its diff restored them, and the closed issue made the reverted state read as the finished one. ([#189](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/189))

### Fixed

- **The engine fingerprint no longer forgets its dependencies when built from a published crate.** A certificate records which engine judged a file, and the engine's identity is a hash over everything that can change a verdict — the rules, plus the crates they run through. `cargo publish` rewrites the packaged manifest and strips the `path` key from every dependency, and the hash found those crates BY that key, so a build from a crates.io tarball covered 14 files in 1 crate instead of 29 across 4, without a word. A consumer who picked up a new `laterite-ags4-parse` — the tokenizer that decides where fields end — would have kept trusting every certificate minted before it. Our own crates are now identified by `name@version` when their sources are not reachable, which is sound precisely there: a published version's content is immutable. The in-workspace fingerprint is unchanged, so no existing certificate is affected. ([#190](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/190))
- **The engine crates build on the Rust version they promise.** Every crate declares `rust-version = "1.85"`, cargo only ever enforces that field on our dependencies and never on us, and so the promise had quietly been false: `laterite-ags4-emit` used a `let` chain, stable in 1.88. A consumer pinned to an older toolchain would have resolved to us precisely because the floor said they could, then failed to compile against our source. The one line is rewritten and the MSRV gate now builds the publish set on whatever floor the manifests declare — read from the manifests rather than restated, so raising the floor cannot leave the gate testing the old one. ([#193](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/193))
- **`laterite` 0.1.2 — the error a bytes caller actually hits now says what to do about it.** Asking for the on-disk file check on bytes reported `cannot validate 210 bytes`: true, and useless. It names the size of the input and nothing about the mistake, and it is the first thing a service validating uploads runs into. It now explains that Rule 20's on-disk half needs a path to look beside, so `check_files` belongs with `validate` rather than `validate_bytes`. `Error`'s `Display` also gained an alternate form: `{}` stays terse because `anyhow` and `eyre` walk `source()` themselves and would otherwise print the cause twice, while `{:#}` appends it for callers using neither — which the field's own documentation had claimed since the crate was written. No public signature changed. ([#201](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/201))
- **Four crates that ship as products were left on the engine version.** `laterite-py`, `laterite-node` and `laterite-ags4-wasm` still said `version.workspace = true` after the tiers split, which was harmless for exactly as long as the two numbers stayed equal and would have broken at the first product-only release. The sharpest case: `wasm-pack` writes the published npm manifest FROM the crate version and the release workflow then asserts the `wasm-v<tag>` matches it, so a `wasm-v0.9.1` tag against a crate still on engine 0.9.0 fails its own tag check. Node's `version()` export would likewise have told callers a number that was not the package they installed. All four now carry the product number, and the gate names the consequence for each rather than asserting they merely ought to match. ([#203](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/203))
- **The surface census had a gate that could never pass, so nothing ran it.** `tools/gen_census.py --check` is what stops the three `lat` launchers drifting apart — it was written after `lat merge` shipped in the native binary and never reached the uvx or npx launchers with every gate green. But its renderer emitted a `repo_ref` to `tests/test_census_faithful.py`, a file that has never existed in this repository, and the wiki lint's dead-reference scan is hard over live content — so the rendered page had that line stripped by hand, which made `--check` report the page stale on every run, forever. An unpassable check does not get wired into CI, and it wasn't: no job invoked it, so the census could drift from the launchers in silence, which is the exact failure it was built to catch. The false reference is gone, `--check` passes with no change to the committed page or SSOT, and ci.yml's python job now runs it — a step rather than a test, because the check needs BUILT launchers and a test would have had to skip without them. ([#207](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/207))
- **`censor`'s leak-safe default is now held by a test.** Omitting `selectedCodes` applies the policy to EVERY classified heading — the wider scrub, so forgetting the option over-redacts rather than leaving coordinates in the file. The behaviour was correct and entirely unguarded: it sat inside an export no native test could call, and inverting it passed the whole suite. ([#211](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/211))
- **`build_ags4` and `build_ags4_ipc` now return `null` for an absent `line`, as their published types always said.** `BuildReport`'s `.d.ts` declares `line: number | null` on `EmitFinding` and `AppliedFix`, but these two doors serialised through serde-wasm-bindgen's *default* serializer, which writes `undefined` for an absent `Option` — so a consumer writing `f.line === null` type-checked clean and never matched. Every other export in the package already used the json-compatible serializer; there is now only one, and a test refuses to compile a second into the crate. **This is an observable change**: code testing `f.line === undefined` needs `=== null` (or `== null`, which was always correct for both). `?? ` and truthiness checks are unaffected. Verified surgical — the build payload carries no maps and no 64-bit integers, so `None` handling is the only thing the two serializers disagree on. ([#212](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/212), [#213](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/213))

## [0.9.0] — 2026-07-30

The browser API breaks: every `@laterite/ags4-wasm` export now takes an options object instead of a positional tail. And a synthesised `TRAN` is the caller's to supply — the placeholder the emitter used to invent satisfied Rule 14, so files could assert a transmission that never happened and pass validation doing it.

### Added

- **A transmission can carry a description and remarks.** `TranStamp` takes optional `description` and `remarks` (`TRAN_DESC` / `TRAN_REM`), emitted only when set. `TRAN_AGS`, `TRAN_DLIM` and `TRAN_RCON` remain derived and are deliberately not accepted from callers — they describe the syntax of the bytes the emitter is writing, so a supplied value could only contradict them. ([#178](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/178))
- **The browser's `merge` accepts `dictVersion`**, so an edition can be forced from wasm as it always could from Python, Node and the CLI. This gap was found by the new cross-surface knob gate on its first run — the browser had simply never been held to the same option set as the other surfaces. ([#182](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/182))
- **The browser package ships its own result types.** `validate`, `build_ags4`, `build_ags4_ipc`, `censor` and `ParsedDataset.meta` were typed `any` in the generated `.d.ts`, so every consumer had to re-describe the report shape by hand — a downstream browser consumer reported `build_ags4` returning `any` as a defect. The crate now publishes `ValidationReport`, `RuleGroup`, `FindingDto`, `ValErr`, `BuildReport`, `EmitFinding`, `AppliedFix`, `CensorResult`, `CensorTally` and `GroupMeta`, so **you can delete your copy**. Two tests bind the published interfaces to the Rust serde structs and the `AppliedFix` unions to the validator's enums, so they cannot drift into being prettier `any`. `diff`, `compute_fixes` and `dictionary` still return `any`: their shapes belong to other crates, and hand-mirroring them here would rebuild the very problem this removes. ([#185](https://github.com/niko86/laterite/pull/185))

### Changed

- **Breaking: every `@laterite/ags4-wasm` export takes an options object.** `validate`, `certify`, `build_ags4`, `build_ags4_ipc` and `merge` had grown positional tails of up to nine arguments, where `undefined, undefined, true` was an ordinary thing to write and slot order was the only thing keeping it correct.
